newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb leader rebuffs offer by Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb leader rebuffs offer by Milosevic.

text.p: Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic has spurned an offer from Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to mediate in a tense power struggle with her hardline nationalist opponents.
Plavsic's aides said on Tuesday evening she had "nothing to discuss" with Milosevic, who armed and directed the Bosnian Serbs during more than three years of war.
The Belgrade news agency Beta quoted Plavsic's supporters as saying she considered Milosevic responsible for "the destruction of everything worthy in Serbdom".
Milosevic invited the Bosnian Serb president and her rival Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's multi-ethnic collective presidency, to Belgrade for talks to resolve their conflict.

Plavsic and hardliners led by Krajisnik and ex-president Radovan Karazdic, an indicted war criminal, have been locked in a power struggle for more than a week since she accused them of large-scale corruption.
Milosevic said the "crisis must be solved through cooperation," Tanjug news agency in Serbian-led Yugoslavia reported.
Diplomats say the Serbian leader has rebuilt links with Karadzic and his allies since he forced them to sign the Dayton peace agreement against their will in 1995.
Karadzic has travelled to Belgrade more than once this year to hold talks with Milosevic, who has often relished the role of kingmaker among the Bosnian Serbs.
Plavsic has never enjoyed warm relations with the Serbian leader, accusing him of betraying the nationalist goal to carve out a "Greater Serbia" in former Yugoslavia.

Plavsic once publicly refused to shake Milosevic's hand when he lobbied the Bosnian Serbs to accept an earlier peace plan in 1993. His police later prevented her from crossing the Bosnia-Serbia border.

NATO leaders meeting in Madrid on Tuesday demanded Karadzic loyalists respect Plavsic's decision to dissolve parliament and warned that the alliance-led peace force would not tolerate any attempt to resolve the crisis through violence.
Plavsic has accused Karadzic's circle of plundering Serb territory through smuggling rackets and has advocated cooperation with Western peacemakers to win reconstruction aid.

With parliament dissolved, Plavsic will soon have the option of forming a new government. Diplomats said two competing authorities in Serb territory could emerge, one in the west and one directed by Karadzic in the east.
She won promises from Bosnian Serb army generals on Tuesday that they would remain neutral in the conflict after talks in the northwest town of Banja Luka.
Purged by hardliners and lacking financial support, the army is overshadowed by a well-funded, large police force controlled by Karadzic.

Plavsic dissolved parliament last week and called for new elections on September 1. The hardliners dismissed her decision and held a session of the assembly anyway, rewriting laws to enable her to be recalled and to strip her of defence powers.
Karadzic's efforts to crush Plavsic have focused attention on his persistent influence and the failure of the major powers to arrest him and other indicted war criminals.
The former Sarajevo psychiatrist was forced out of public office last year under international pressure when he promised to stay out of the political arena.

At the NATO summit in Madrid, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright gave no indication that the United States and its allies were prepared if necessary to send troops to arrest indicted war criminals.
But Albright said: "I think the point is... there is no statute of limitations on their crimes and their day will come."
